prompt: Equivalence of advanced data structures — which two statements are correct?
options: Every binary max-heap can be coloured as a Red-Black tree.
Every Red-Black tree is a binary search tree.
Every Red-Black tree is an AVL tree.
Every AVL tree can be coloured as a Red-Black tree.
explanation: A Red-Black tree is by definition a BST plus colouring ✓. AVL's stricter height bound (≈1.44·log n) always fits inside the RBT bound (2·log(n+1)), so every AVL tree admits a valid RB colouring ✓ — a classic textbook result. The converse fails: an RBT may be less balanced than AVL permits ✗. And a max-heap is not even a BST, so no colouring can make it one ✗.

prompt: Rotations (rotateLeft() / rotateRight()) in trees — which two structures need *no* rotation function when inserting?
options: Splay trees need no rotation function on insert.
AVL trees need no rotation function on insert.
Binary search trees need no rotation function on insert.
Binary max-heaps need no rotation function on insert.
explanation: A plain BST insert just descends and attaches a leaf ✓, and heap insert restores the heap property with sift-up *swaps* along one path, not rotations ✓. Splay trees rotate on every access including insert ✗, and AVL trees rotate to rebalance ✗.

prompt: A node in an AVL tree has left subtree height 4 and right subtree height 1. Which statement is correct?
options: This is always valid — AVL only constrains the root.
This is invalid: the balance factor of 3 violates the |bf| ≤ 1 invariant.
This is valid only for the root.
This is valid as long as the tree has fewer than 10 nodes.
explanation: AVL requires bf(x) = height(x.left) − height(x.right) ∈ {−1, 0, 1} for *every* node. Here bf = 3, so the subtree must be rebalanced by rotation. (In practice AVL never lets |bf| exceed 2, because it repairs imbalance the moment it appears.)

prompt: The AVL balance invariant — which two statements are correct?
options: bf(x) = height(x.left) − height(x.right), and by convention an empty subtree has height −1, so a leaf has height 0.
|bf(x)| = 2 is the only trigger for a rotation; bf ∈ {−1, 0, 1} is valid.
AVL guarantees a height of at most 2·log(n+1), the same bound as a Red-Black tree.
The invariant only has to hold along the path from the root to the deepest leaf.
explanation: The definition with height(∅) = −1 ✓ and the |bf| = 2 trigger ✓ are exactly as in the lecture. AVL's bound is the *tighter* ≈1.44·log(n+2) ✗, and the invariant must hold at every single node ✗.

prompt: During an AVL insert, node a has bf(a) = 2 and bf(a.left) = 1. Which case is this and what is the fix?
options: LL case: a single rotateRight(a)
LR case: rotateLeft(a.left), then rotateRight(a)
RR case: a single rotateLeft(a)
RL case: rotateRight(a.right), then rotateLeft(a)
explanation: bf(a) > 1 means left-heavy; bf(a.left) ≥ 0 (here +1) means the imbalance continues on the *same* side (left-left). A single rotateRight(a) restores balance. The LR case would need bf(a.left) < 0.

prompt: During an AVL insert, node a has bf(a) = −2 and bf(a.right) = 1. Which case is this and what is the fix?
options: RR case: a single rotateLeft(a)
LL case: a single rotateRight(a)
RL case: rotateRight(a.right), then rotateLeft(a)
LR case: rotateLeft(a.left), then rotateRight(a)
explanation: bf(a) < −1 means right-heavy; bf(a.right) > 0 means that child is itself left-heavy, so the imbalance zig-zags (right-left). The double rotation rotateRight(a.right) followed by rotateLeft(a) is required — a single rotation would not fix it.

prompt: AVL insert versus AVL delete — which two statements are correct?
options: Insert needs at most one single or double rotation in total, because the rotation restores the subtree's pre-insertion height.
Delete may need rebalancing at every level up to the root, because a rotation there can *shrink* the subtree's height.
Delete, like insert, may stop after the first rotation.
Delete uses a different rotation primitive than insert.
explanation: After an insert rotation the subtree height equals what it was before the insert, so no ancestor can become unbalanced ⟹ break ✓. After a delete rotation the height can decrease, propagating a new imbalance upward ⟹ up to O(log n) rotations, no early break ✓✗. Both use the same rotateLeft/rotateRight primitives ✗.

prompt: AVL versus Red-Black trees as a design trade-off — which two statements are correct?
options: AVL's stricter balance makes lookups slightly faster but rebalancing on writes more frequent.
Both guarantee Θ(log n) for search, insert and delete in the worst case.
AVL stores a colour bit per node; Red-Black trees store a height per node.
Red-Black trees rebalance on every read access, AVL trees do not.
explanation: The read-vs-write trade-off ✓ and the shared Θ(log n) worst case ✓ are the key comparison points. The stored metadata is swapped in option 3 — AVL stores heights/balance factors, RBTs store colours ✗ — and neither rebalances on a pure read; that is the splay tree ✗.

prompt: The LR/RL double rotation — which two statements are correct?
options: It is just two single rotations back-to-back around different pivots; no separate primitive is needed.
In the LR case the inner rotation is applied to a.left first, and only then is a itself rotated.
It requires a dedicated rotateDouble primitive that cannot be expressed via rotateLeft/rotateRight.
In the LR case a is rotated first, and only then a.left.
explanation: A double rotation decomposes into two singles ✓, and the LR fix is rotateLeft(a.left) *then* rotateRight(a) ✓ — the inner (child) rotation converts the zig-zag into a straight line so the outer rotation can finish the job. Reversing that order ✗ or inventing a new primitive ✗ is wrong.
